sections.text: Mastoparan-S from Sphodromantis viridis exhibits antimicrobial activity by disrupting bacterial membranes

The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance underscores the urgent need for alternative treatments. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are considered viable substitutes for conventional antibiotics due to their broad-spectrum activity and unique mechanisms of action. AMPs are an integral component of the innate immune system in invertebrates. Mastoparan-S, a 14-amino acid AMP originally identified in the praying mantis Sphodromantis viridis reportedly exhibits antimicrobial activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, as well as fungi. In this study, the antibacterial activity and mechanism of action of chemically-synthesized mastoparan-S are evaluated against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa . Mastoparan-S exhibits potent antibacterial activity against S. aureus and P. aeruginosa, without inducing cytotoxicity or hemolytic activity in RAW264.7 or HaCaT cells. Mastoparan-S effectively inhibits biofilm formation by S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. Mechanistically, mastopran-S kills bacteria by disrupting the bacterial membrane. Collectively, these findings suggest that mastoparan-S is a potential therapeutic agent for treating S. aureus and P. aeruginosa infections. Introduction Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a significant global health threat in the twenty-first century. The misuse and overuse of antimicrobials contribute to the rapid increase in AMR. While antimicrobial use, even when medically necessary, can lead to resistance development, indiscriminate and excessive use greatly accelerates the emergence and spread of resistant pathogens. Globally, AMR is associated with higher morbidity and mortality (Ayukekbong et al. 2017 ). The World Health Organization (WHO) warns that antibiotic resistance is increasing globally, and the effectiveness of antibiotics in treating infections is decreasing, potentially leading to untreatable bacterial diseases (Erdem Büyükkiraz and Kesmen 2022 ). By 2050, it is projected that untreatable infectious diseases will result in 10 million deaths due to a decline in antibiotic development. Given the limited availability of effective treatments, lack of successful preventive strategies, and scarcity of new antibiotics, innovative therapeutic approaches and antimicrobial strategies are urgently needed (Khayat et al. 2022 ). Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are major causes of infections like pneumonia and sepsis and contributors to the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. These gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, respectively (Fischer et al. 2021 ), belong to the ESKAPE group ( Enterococcus faecium, S. aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, P. aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species)—pathogens distinguished by their multidrug resistance and involvement in life-threatening infections (Mlynarczyk-Bonikowska et al. 2022 ). Individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) or chronic wounds are particularly vulnerable to infections caused by opportunistic pathogens. CF patients with concurrent P. aeruginosa and S. aureus infections experience more severe disease progression and worse clinical prognosis than those with monoinfections (Orazi et al. 2019 ). Hence, antibiotics capable of eradicating S. aureus and P. aeruginosa are required. The ability to resist infections is based on the innate immune system, which enables rapid and comprehensive defense against invading pathogens (Manniello et al. 2021 ). Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), i.e., host defense peptides, are small bioactive molecules primarily produced by multicellular organisms, including insects, through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions (Lazzaro et al. 2020 ). AMP can rapidly eliminate gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, fungi, parasites, and viruses (Mahlapuu et al. 2020 ). In contrast to conventional antibiotics, AMPs' positively charged residues interact with and disrupt negatively charged bacterial membranes, reducing resistance (Shi et al. 2022 ). Due to their therapeutic effects, low risk of resistance, and fewer side effects, AMPs have emerged as potent alternatives to antibiotics. Mastoparan-S, isolated from the mantis Sphodromantis viridis , exhibits antibacterial and antifungal effects against Escherichia coli , K. pneumoniae , P. aeruginosa , and C. albicans without causing cytotoxicity or hemolysis (Zare-Zardini et al. 2015 ). However, its antimicrobial activity and mechanism of action against S. aureus and P. aeruginosa remain unclear. In this study, the antimicrobial activity and mechanism of action of mastoparan-S against S. aureus and P. aeruginosa are investigated. Additionally, the toxicity of mastoparan-S toward red blood cells (RBCs), as well as HaCaT and RAW 264.7 cells from human keratinocytes and murine macrophages, respectively, was assessed. The native amino acid sequence of S. viridis mastoparan-S was used without structural modifications or rational design. The findings of this study suggest that mastoparan-S possesses potent antimicrobial and anti-biofilm activities against S. aureus and P. aeruginosa , primarily through membrane-targeted mechanisms.

Material and methods Materials Defibrinated sheep blood cells were purchased from MB Cells (Los Angeles, CA, USA). Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazole-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT), N-phenyl-1-naphthylamine (NPN), 3,3′-dipropylthiadicarbocyanine iodide (DiSC₃(5)), propidium iodide (PI), and ciprofloxacin were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (St Louis, MO, USA). Microbial strains P. aeruginosa (American Type Culture Collection [ATCC] 27853), S. aureus (ATCC 25923), and S. typhimurium (ATCC 14028) were acquired from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). A. baumannii (Korea Collection for Type Cultures [KCTC] 2508), Bacillus cereus (KCTC 1012), Bacillus subtilis (KCTC 2217), and K. pneumoniae (KCTC 2208) were obtained from the Korea Collection for Type Cultures (KCTC). Additionally, P. aeruginosa antibiotic-resistant strains were isolated from patients with otitis media at Chonnam National University Hospital. Peptide synthesis and purification Mastoparan-S was synthesized using the solid-phase 9-fluorenylmethoxycarbonyl (Fmoc) method, as reported previously (Fields and Noble 1990 ), on a Rink amide 4-methylbenzhydrylamine resin using a Liberty microwave peptide synthesizer (CEM; Matthews, NY, USA); 0.45 M 2-(1H-benzotriazole-1-yl)-1,1,3,3-tetramethyluronium hexafluorophosphate (HBTU) dissolved in piperidine/dimethylformamide (DMF), 2 M N,N -diisopropylethylamine (DIEA) dissolved in N -methylpyrrolidone (NMP), and 0.1 M N -hydroxybenzotriazole (HOBt) dissolved in DMF were used as linkage reagents. After washing with dichloromethane (DCM), cleavage was performed by incubation for 2 h at 25 °C in a trifluoroacetic acid (TFE) solution containing water, phenol, and triisopropylsilane. The crude peptide was diluted, mixed with ice-cold diethyl ether, spread onto a tube wall, and dried. Dried mastoparan-S was purified by reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) using a Jupiter C18 column (4.6 × 250 mm, 300 Å, 5 μm; Phenomenex, Torrance, CA, USA). Mastoparan-S was dissolved in deionized water and stored at −20 °C. The mastopran-S had a purity of > 95%. The molecular weight was confirmed by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (MALDI-MS; Kratos Analytical, Chestnut Ridge, NY, USA). Peptide analysis The structures and electrostatic surfaces of PN5 were predicted using PEP-FOLD3 and PyMOL software. Structural parameters were analyzed using the BACHEM peptide calculator tool ( https://www.bachem.com/knowledge-center/peptide-calculator/ ). Secondary structures of the peptides were analyzed using the BESTSEL server. Circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy CD experiments were performed using a JASCO 810 spectropolarimeter (Jasco, Tokyo, Japan) to investigate the secondary structures of the peptides in different environments. A peptide solution (40 μM) was prepared in 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4), 30 mM SDS, and 50% TFE. CD spectra were recorded from 190 to 250 nm using a quartz cell with a 1 mm path length (Gopal et al. 2012 ). Antimicrobial activity Gram-positive, gram-negative, and antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains were cultured at 37 °C in appropriate culture media (Luria–Bertani broth, nutrient broth [NB], tryptic soy broth [TSB], brain heart infusion broth, or Mueller–Hinton broth). The antimicrobial activities of the peptides were determined using a standard microdilution method (Park et al. 2003 ). Bacterial strains were diluted in fresh culture medium to a final concentration of 2 × 10 5 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL. The peptides were serially diluted two-fold from 64 to 1 μM in 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). Peptides were added to duplicate the bacterial suspensions in the mid-logarithmic phase. The absorbance at 600 nm was measured after the mixtures were incubated for 18 h at 37 °C. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was defined as the lowest peptide concentration that completely inhibited bacterial growth. Following MIC assessment, aliquots from the MIC well and two higher concentrations were plated on agar. The lowest concentration showing no visible bacterial colony growth was recorded as the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) for each strain and peptide. Time-kill kinetic assay The kinetics of the peptide’s bactericidal effects against P. aeruginosa KCTC 27853 and S. aureus ATCC 25923 were analyzed. After culturing each strain in an appropriate medium, 2 × 10 5 CFU/mL suspensions were incubated with 1 × MIC, 2 × MIC, and 4 × MIC of the peptide in sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) at 37 °C. Aliquots of each sample were plated on appropriate agar plates and incubated overnight at 37 °C, after which the colonies were counted. Biofilm inhibition assay Bacterial suspensions were diluted in fresh culture media containing 0.2% glucose to a final concentration of 5 × 10 5 CFU/mL; 90 μL of each suspension was placed in a 96-well plate. A two-fold serially diluted peptide (10 μL) was added and incubated for 24 h at 37 °C. The culture medium was removed, and cells were fixed with 100% methanol for 15 min. After removing the methanol, the samples were air-dried, and cells were stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 30 min. Cells were washed with distilled water, and 95% ethanol was added to dissolve the biofilm; the absorbance was recorded at 595 nm using a Versa-Max microplate ELISA reader (Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA, USA). To visualize the peptide’s effect on biofilm formation, S. aureus and P. aeruginosa biofilms were fixed with 100% methanol and stained with SYTO9 (1 μM) dye for 30 min in the dark. Images were obtained using an EVOS FL Auto 2 fluorescence microscope. Hemolysis assay Defibrinated sheep RBCs were centrifuged at 800 × g for 10 min and washed thrice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). The peptides were serially diluted two-fold in PBS. Subsequently, 100 μL of the peptide was added to a 96-well plate, and 100 μL of sheep red blood cells, at a final concentration of 8%, were added and incubated with gentle agitation for 1 h at 37 °C. The mixture was centrifuged at 800 × g for 5 min, and the supernatant was transferred to a new 96-well plate. Absorbance was measured at 414 nm. Hemolytic activity and cytotoxicity of mastoparan-S The clinical translation of peptides is hampered by hemolysis and cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells. Therefore, mastoparan-S’s effects were evaluated in vitro [9]. Within the tested 3.13–200 µM range, mastoparan-S did not induce hemolysis. In contrast, the positive control melittin induced 57% hemolysis at 6.25 μM (Fig. 2 C). Mastoparan-S induced cytotoxicity in 7% and 83% of RAW 264.7 cells at 100 and 200 µM, respectively. Melittin induced approximately 73% cell death in RAW 264.7 cells at 12.5 μM (Fig. 2 D). Meanwhile, 200 µM Mastoparan-S and melittin induced cell death in approximately 26% and 85% of HaCaT cells, respectively (Fig. 2 E). These findings suggest that mastoparan-S is a safe and effective antibacterial agent.

Discussion Antibiotics are commonly used to prevent and treat bacterial infections. Bacteria can develop antibiotic resistance when exposed to antibiotics, making treatment ineffective. Consequently, infections become harder to treat, and disease transmission, severe illness, and mortality can increase (Chinemerem Nwobodo et al. 2022 ). With the decline in antibiotic efficacy against common bacterial infections, the development of new drugs has decreased, posing a significant threat to global health (Haroon et al. 2020 ). S. aureus and P. aeruginosa are the leading causative agents of severe nosocomial infections. These bacteria are classified as ESKAPE pathogens and the WHO has identified them as priority antibiotic-resistant organisms necessitating the prompt development of new antimicrobial therapies (Sabat et al. 2021 ). To address these challenges, novel non-antibiotic therapies are required. AMPs are small proteins that possess antibacterial, antiviral and antifungal properties. They constitute a class of bioactive molecules ranging in length from 6 to 50 amino acids, exhibiting structural and functional diversity (Gonçalves et al. 2025 ). AMPs are ubiquitous in multicellular eukaryotes, with numerous distinct AMP genes expressed in the epithelial tissues of most plant and animal species, particularly in response to infections (Lazzaro et al. 2020 ). The mechanisms underlying the action of AMPs include the disruption of bacterial membranes, modulation of immune responses, and binding to intracellular targets such as nucleic acids (Huang and Li 2023 ). Unlike conventional antibiotics, AMPs disrupt multiple pathogen targets and significantly reduce drug resistance (Xuan et al. 2023 ). Mastoparan-S, a 14-residue AMP derived from the praying mantis S. viridis , belongs to the mastoparan family based on its structural characteristics. It exhibits antimicrobial effects against a broad range of microorganisms, including gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, with greater potency than kanamycin based on lower MIC values. This study demonstrated the antimicrobial activity of mastoparan-S against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, including drug-resistant S. aureus and P. aeruginosa , while similar effects were not achieved by ciprofloxacin. In contrast, mastoparan-S showed minimal cytotoxicity in RAW 264.7 and HaCaT cells at 200 μM, with approximately 83% and 26% cell death, respectively. In a previous study, mastoparan-S exhibited cytotoxicity at concentrations above 40 μg/mL (24.7 μM), with less than 10% cytotoxicity observed in HeLa cells, a human epithelial cell line derived from cervical adenocarcinoma. The discrepancy with the current study may be due to differences in cell line sensitivity or experimental conditions. These findings support its potential safety in non-cancerous and immune-related cell types. Melittin, a cationic amphiphilic peptide and the principal component of bee venom, exhibits antitumor, antiviral, and anti-inflammatory activities in vitro and in vivo (Zhang et al. 2024 ). However, mastoparan-S exhibited significantly lower hemolytic and cytotoxic activities than melittin in vitro. Bacterial membranes comprise a lipid bilayer with a hydrophobic core formed by fatty acid tails, carrying a negative surface charge due to ionized phosphate and carboxyl groups (Wilhelm et al. 2021 ). AMPs disrupt bacterial membranes through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions. In the current study, the structure of mastoparan-S was predicted in membrane-mimicking environments using SDS and TFE to represent a negatively charged surface and a hydrophobic environment, respectively. Generally, AMPs exhibit α-helical, ß-sheet, or random coil structures (Nguyen et al. 2011 ). The predicted structure of mastoparan-S was confirmed by CD spectroscopy to adopt a random coil structure in an aqueous solution and an α-helical conformation in a membrane-mimicking environment. LPS is the major component of the outer leaflet of the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, while LTA is a key component of the cell wall of gram-positive bacteria (Szentirmai et al. 2021 ). LTA and LPS are strong stimuli for the host inflammatory response. AMPs can bind LTA and LPS via electrostatic interactions, facilitating initial binding to the bacterial surface and potentially influencing AMP conformation and activity. Thus, their roles extend beyond membrane recognition and may affect the antimicrobial mechanism (Lee et al. 2017 ). In the present study, CD spectra indicate mastoparan-S forms an α-helical structure when interacting with LTA and LPS. This suggests mastoparan-S can neutralize LTA and LPS and inhibit their ability to activate the immune response. Future research should explore the potential of mastoparan-S to neutralize LTA and LPS and attenuate inflammatory responses in cellular models. Gram-negative bacteria are characterized by a peptidoglycan cell wall enclosed in an outer membrane containing LPS, which acts as a barrier against toxins like antibiotics (Ebbensgaard et al. 2018 ). Therefore, disrupting the integrity of the outer membrane is a key approach to combating antibiotic resistance and developing therapeutic approaches. NPN assays confirmed that mastoparan-S disrupted the outer membrane of P. aeruginosa . In bacteria, a reduction in the membrane potential, known as membrane depolarization, can compromise cell viability by impairing vital functions and enhancing membrane permeability. Mastoparan-S induced membrane depolarization in S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. Mechanistically, it exerts antimicrobial activity by forming pores (~ 2.8 nm) in bacterial cell membranes. In summary, mastoparan-S exerts antimicrobial effects primarily by disrupting bacterial membranes. The peptide adopts an α-helical structure in bacterial membrane-like environments, facilitating its interaction with negatively charged components such as LTA and LPS. Additionally, mastoparan-S demonstrates minimal hemolytic and cytotoxic effects in vitro. Collectively, these findings suggest that mastoparan-S is a promising candidate for developing antibiotics to combat multidrug-resistant bacterial infections.

In a previous study, mastoparan-S exhibited cytotoxicity at concentrations above 40 μg/mL (24.7 μM), with less than 10% cytotoxicity observed in HeLa cells, a human epithelial cell line derived from cervical adenocarcinoma. The discrepancy with the current study may be due to differences in cell line sensitivity or experimental conditions. These findings support its potential safety in non-cancerous and immune-related cell types. Melittin, a cationic amphiphilic peptide and the principal component of bee venom, exhibits antitumor, antiviral, and anti-inflammatory activities in vitro and in vivo (Zhang et al. 2024 ). However, mastoparan-S exhibited significantly lower hemolytic and cytotoxic activities than melittin in vitro.

Bacterial membranes comprise a lipid bilayer with a hydrophobic core formed by fatty acid tails, carrying a negative surface charge due to ionized phosphate and carboxyl groups (Wilhelm et al. 2021 ). AMPs disrupt bacterial membranes through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions. In the current study, the structure of mastoparan-S was predicted in membrane-mimicking environments using SDS and TFE to represent a negatively charged surface and a hydrophobic environment, respectively. Generally, AMPs exhibit α-helical, ß-sheet, or random coil structures (Nguyen et al. 2011 ). The predicted structure of mastoparan-S was confirmed by CD spectroscopy to adopt a random coil structure in an aqueous solution and an α-helical conformation in a membrane-mimicking environment.

LPS is the major component of the outer leaflet of the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, while LTA is a key component of the cell wall of gram-positive bacteria (Szentirmai et al. 2021 ). LTA and LPS are strong stimuli for the host inflammatory response. AMPs can bind LTA and LPS via electrostatic interactions, facilitating initial binding to the bacterial surface and potentially influencing AMP conformation and activity. Thus, their roles extend beyond membrane recognition and may affect the antimicrobial mechanism (Lee et al. 2017 ). In the present study, CD spectra indicate mastoparan-S forms an α-helical structure when interacting with LTA and LPS. This suggests mastoparan-S can neutralize LTA and LPS and inhibit their ability to activate the immune response. Future research should explore the potential of mastoparan-S to neutralize LTA and LPS and attenuate inflammatory responses in cellular models.

Gram-negative bacteria are characterized by a peptidoglycan cell wall enclosed in an outer membrane containing LPS, which acts as a barrier against toxins like antibiotics (Ebbensgaard et al. 2018 ). Therefore, disrupting the integrity of the outer membrane is a key approach to combating antibiotic resistance and developing therapeutic approaches. NPN assays confirmed that mastoparan-S disrupted the outer membrane of P. aeruginosa . In bacteria, a reduction in the membrane potential, known as membrane depolarization, can compromise cell viability by impairing vital functions and enhancing membrane permeability. Mastoparan-S induced membrane depolarization in S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. Mechanistically, it exerts antimicrobial activity by forming pores (~ 2.8 nm) in bacterial cell membranes.

In summary, mastoparan-S exerts antimicrobial effects primarily by disrupting bacterial membranes. The peptide adopts an α-helical structure in bacterial membrane-like environments, facilitating its interaction with negatively charged components such as LTA and LPS. Additionally, mastoparan-S demonstrates minimal hemolytic and cytotoxic effects in vitro. Collectively, these findings suggest that mastoparan-S is a promising candidate for developing antibiotics to combat multidrug-resistant bacterial infections.
